rv.q: Punched in the stomach, but equipped with a new pair of contact lenses. It is a long time since I left a theatre feeling as I did after seeing Machinal. Richard Jones has directed a skewering production of Sophie Treadwell’s 1928 play, which is generally hailed as a masterpiece of theatrical expressionism.

It is a masterclass in how to play a character at the end of her tether. Sheehy is matched with a stellar supporting cast: Tim Frances does well to make her husband seem a warm and avuncular figure yet, at the same time, clearly bad news for her while Pierro Niel-Mee excels at making her lover – the Young Man – a slightly slippery charmer.

It doesn’t reach the sides of the huge Old Vic stage. It’s boxed in, like its protagonist, Young Woman, whose actual name of Helen will only come out once she reaches the courtroom. She struggles to feel like herself at the office, in her mother’s kitchen, in a speakeasy, on honeymoon, giving birth.
You rarely see such meticulous, detailed work in the theatre.
